ox: Correct. Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan wall on the outside and no outer membrane. The thick wall traps the crystal violet dye, so they stain purple.
Wrong. This is Gram-negative bacteria, which have a thin peptidoglycan layer and an outer membrane holding LPS (lipopolysaccharide). Trap: mixing up the two groups.
Wrong. Almost all bacteria have a wall. Mycoplasma is the famous exception. Trap: choosing the exception instead of the rule.
Wrong. Gram-negative cells stain pink or red because the thin wall loses the purple dye. Trap: remembering pink and linking it to the wrong group.

p: The Gram stain sorts bacteria by their cell wall. Peptidoglycan is a mesh of sugars and amino acids that gives the wall strength.
Gram-positive: thick peptidoglycan, no outer membrane, stains purple. Gram-negative: thin peptidoglycan, plus an outer membrane with LPS, stains pink.

q23.eli: A thick winter coat holds the dye in like a sponge. A thin jacket lets it wash out.
mem: Gram-positive = thick wall, purple, no outer membrane.
Gram-negative = thin wall, pink, outer membrane with LPS.
q23.trap: Swapping the colors. Positive keeps the purple stain; negative loses it and shows pink.
q23.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (microbiology and biology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Wrong. Transformation is when a bacterium picks up free, naked DNA from its surroundings. No virus is involved. Trap: both move DNA, so they sound alike.
Correct. In transduction, a bacteriophage (a virus that infects bacteria) carries bacterial DNA from one cell to another. The virus is the vector.
Wrong. Conjugation moves DNA directly between two bacteria through a sex pilus (a tube-like bridge). No virus needed.
Wrong. Binary fission is how a bacterium divides into two copies. It does not transfer DNA between different cells.

p: Bacteria share genes in three ways. Each has a different carrier.
Transformation: free DNA from the environment. Transduction: a bacteriophage carries the DNA. Conjugation: a direct bridge (sex pilus) between two cells.

q24.eli: Transduction is like a mail carrier (the virus) delivering a package (DNA) from one house to another.
mem: Binary fission = reproduction, not gene transfer.
q24.mn: Transduction has the word 'duct' like a delivery tube: a virus delivers the DNA.
q24.trap: Mixing up transformation and transduction. Look for the word 'bacteriophage' or 'virus' to pick transduction.
q24.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (microbiology and genetics texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. Reverse transcriptase is an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase. It reads the viral RNA and builds a DNA copy.
Wrong. Integrase inserts the finished DNA copy into the host genome. It comes after the copy is made. Trap: both enzymes are retrovirus steps.
Wrong. RNA replicase copies RNA into RNA, which is used by some other RNA viruses. A retrovirus needs RNA to DNA.
Wrong. DNA polymerase I in bacteria removes RNA primers and fills gaps. It reads a DNA template, not an RNA genome.

p: A retrovirus (like HIV) stores its genes as RNA. The host cell reads DNA, so the virus needs to convert its RNA to DNA first.
Reverse transcriptase does this conversion. Then integrase puts the DNA into the host chromosome, where it is copied as a normal gene.

q25.eli: It is like translating a message from a foreign language into the language the town speaks, so the locals can use it.
mem: Integrase: inserts viral DNA into the host genome.
Retroviruses go RNA to DNA to RNA to protein.
q25.trap: Choosing integrase. It joins DNA into the genome but does not make the DNA from RNA.
q25.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (virology and molecular biology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.
